opus-5.5.text:
Well, it goes back to 1994, 1995, when the web was brand new. My students and I at USC had just built one of the first robots you could control over the internet, and we were fascinated by the idea that anyone, anywhere, could reach through their browser and affect something real in the physical world. But we wanted to do it in a way that wasn't just a technical demo.

A garden felt like the perfect counterpoint. The internet was all about speed, instant gratification, clicking and getting a result immediately. A garden is the opposite: it's slow, it's patient, it requires care over weeks and months. So putting those two things together created this interesting tension. People would log in, move the industrial robot arm, plant a seed, water it, and then they had to keep coming back to see if anything grew.

What surprised us was the community that formed around it. Thousands of people became members, they started talking to each other in the chat area, negotiating over space, worrying about who was overwatering. It became a little society organized around this tiny plot of soil.

And underneath it all was a philosophical question I've been chewing on ever since, which I started calling telepistemology: how do you know that what you're seeing through the screen is real? There was no way, really, for someone on the other side of the world to verify that there was an actual garden. They had to trust it. I think that question about trust and mediated reality has only become more pressing with deepfakes and AI-generated content. So the Telegarden was art, but it was also a way of asking what the internet would do to our sense of what's real and how we relate to nature and to each other.

r001.rationale: The response presents the garden’s slow, patient care as a counterpoint to the internet’s speed and instant gratification, making that contrast part of the artwork’s appeal.

r002.rationale: It says remote users could move the robot arm, plant seeds, and water the garden, emphasizing that they acted on a physical environment rather than only viewing it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it came out of a few things colliding at once. This was the mid-nineties, and the web was brand new. Most people had never touched it, and the ones who had were mostly looking at static pages, text and the occasional image. And I'd been working with robots for years, mostly in industrial settings, factory automation, that kind of thing. So I was interested in the question of what happens when you put a robot on the internet. Can you let people on the other side of the world actually act on the physical world, not just look at it?

We'd done an earlier project, the Mercury Project, where people could excavate with a robot arm in a sandbox, kind of an archaeology metaphor. And that worked, people were fascinated. But it was a little barren. It didn't have life in it. And I remember thinking, what if instead of digging, the robot could tend something that grows? A garden is about the most patient, slow, physical thing you can imagine. It's the opposite of the internet, which is fast and ephemeral. So putting those two together felt like a productive tension.

What really appealed to me was that it wasn't a demonstration of technology so much as a question. People from all over the world could log in, plant a seed, water it, watch it over weeks and months. And a community formed around it, people who'd never met, arguing about whether someone had overwatered the basil. There was a sort of commons problem built right in. One person's water affects everyone's plants. That was very much the point.

And there was a skeptical layer too. Because you're looking at a picture on a screen, you can't actually verify there's a garden. We called that "telepistemology," the question of what you can know at a distance. People would ask, how do I know this is real? And I'd say, that's exactly the right question. The internet was about to make that question central to everyone's life, and most people hadn't noticed yet. So the garden was sincere, there really were plants, but the doubt was part of the artwork.

r001.rationale: The response calls the garden “slow” and “physical,” contrasts it with the internet as “fast and ephemeral,” and says combining them felt artistically productive.

r002.rationale: It contrasts acting on the physical world with merely looking at it, and describes remote users planting seeds and watering the garden.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me was the contrast between the internet and gardening. The internet invites you to move quickly, to jump from one thing to another. A garden asks you to slow down, pay attention, and care for something over time. Putting a robot between those two worlds made that contrast tangible.

And the fact that it was a physical garden mattered. You weren’t just manipulating an image on a screen; your actions had consequences for something living. That raises questions about responsibility and about sharing a space with people you may never meet. What does it mean to care for a garden together at a distance?

There’s also a question about knowledge: if your experience of the garden comes through a camera and a network, how do you know what’s really there? I liked that the technology could become a way of asking those questions, rather than simply being the subject of the artwork.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the internet with gardening, then describes a physical, living garden and a robot connecting those worlds.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes acting on a living garden from manipulating an image on a screen and describes caring for that garden together at a distance.

sol-6.1.text:
What appealed to me was the contrast. The internet seemed to promise that everything could happen instantly, and a garden asks you to slow down. You can send a command to a robot, but you can’t make a seed grow any faster. You have to come back, pay attention, and care for something over time.

And I liked the idea that this wasn’t just an image of a garden. There was a physical place, with living plants, and your actions at a distance could affect it. That raises a wonderful question: How do you know what’s really on the other end of your connection? You see an image, you move the robot, you see another image—but your experience is always mediated.

Then there’s the social aspect. You’re sharing this little patch of earth with other people. So an interface that initially looks like an opportunity to control a robot becomes an invitation to cooperate and take care of something together.

r001.rationale: The response describes the garden’s slow, living physicality as contrasting with the internet’s promise of instant action, and presents that contrast as part of the appeal.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the work from merely seeing an image by saying users can move the robot and their distant actions affect a real place with living plants.
